title: Consensus (Raft)
subtitle: Watch five servers agree on one write, lose their leader, elect a new one, and never lose a committed entry.
learn: Why a group of machines needs consensus instead of one trusted copy
How Raft elects a leader using terms, randomized timeouts and majority votes
How log replication and majority commit make a write durable
Why a minority partition can never commit and a stale leader is forced to step down
What etcd and ZooKeeper use consensus for, and what they are not for

steps.title: Who decides what is true?
steps.body: Say you keep a cluster's critical settings, such as which node owns which job, on one server. That server dies and everything stops. So you keep copies on five servers. Now a harder problem appears. If two clients write different values at the same moment, or a server crashes mid-write, how do all five end up agreeing on one history? Making machines agree despite crashes and lost messages is called consensus.
steps.idea: Copies give you availability. Consensus keeps those copies from disagreeing.
steps.caption: Five servers must act like one reliable machine.

steps.title: One leader, many followers
steps.body: Raft is a popular consensus algorithm. It makes the problem simple by electing one leader. Only the leader accepts writes. Followers copy what the leader sends. Time is cut into numbered terms, like presidential terms: each term has at most one leader. Here S1 leads term 1. Every 100 ms or so it sends tiny heartbeat messages ("I'm still alive") to all followers, as the animation shows.
steps.idea: One leader per term means all writes are ordered in one place, so there is nothing to argue about.
steps.caption: S1 leads term 1 and sends heartbeats to every follower.

steps.title: A write enters the log
steps.body: A client sends set x=5. The leader adds it to its own log, which is an ordered list of commands. It then sends an AppendEntries message to every follower, carrying the entry and its position in the log. Each follower writes the entry to disk before replying. Right now the entry exists but is not committed (not yet safe), so the leader has told the client nothing. Only the leader's own copy exists so far: 1 of the 3 needed.
steps.idea: A log entry is only a proposal until enough servers have stored it.
steps.caption: The leader appends x=5 and sends it to all followers.

steps.title: Majority means committed
steps.body: Followers reply as they finish their disk writes. The moment the leader plus two followers hold the entry, that is 3 of 5, a majority has it. The entry is now committed: it will survive any failure the cluster is built to survive. The leader applies it, tells the client "ok", and lets followers know on its next message. In one data center this takes a few milliseconds, mostly the disk flush.
steps.idea: Committed means a majority has it on disk. Any future leader needs a majority too, so the two groups must overlap and include it.
steps.caption: Three of five have it, so x=5 is committed.

steps.title: The leader dies
steps.body: Now S1 goes silent, from a crash or a long pause. Followers expect a heartbeat every 100 ms or so. If none arrives within the election timeout, a follower assumes the leader is gone and runs for leader, becoming a candidate. The timeout is random for each server, so they do not all fire at the same instant. (etcd defaults: 100 ms heartbeat, 1000 ms election timeout.) Until a new leader exists the cluster accepts no writes. A write sent now waits about a second with etcd defaults.
steps.idea: Followers detect a dead leader by silence. Random timeouts make simultaneous candidates unlikely.
steps.caption: Heartbeats stop. S3's timer runs out first.

steps.title: S3 asks for votes
steps.body: S3's timer fires first. It raises the term to 2, votes for itself, and sends RequestVote messages to the others. Each server gives at most one vote per term, and only to a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own. S2 and S4 say yes. With S3's own vote that is 3 of 5, a majority, so S3 becomes leader of term 2 and starts sending heartbeats at once.
steps.idea: One vote per server per term means there can be at most one leader per term.
steps.caption: S3 wins term 2 with votes from S2 and S4.

steps.title: Committed entries survive
steps.body: Why is x=5 not lost? It sits on a majority, and a winning candidate also needs a majority of votes. Any two majorities of five share at least one server, and that server refuses to vote for a candidate missing x=5. So the new leader always holds every committed entry. What if S1 was only frozen or cut off, not crashed? It still thinks it leads term 1. Its first message from S3 carries term 2, so S1 steps down and becomes a follower; any uncommitted entries it had are overwritten.
steps.idea: Overlapping majorities plus the "log must be up to date" vote rule mean a committed entry can never be voted away.
steps.caption: Stale S1 sees term 2 and becomes a follower.

steps.title: A network partition
steps.body: Now suppose a network split cuts S4 and S5 off from the other three. S1 has rejoined as a follower, so S1, S2 and S3 are a majority of 3 and keep working with S3 as leader. S4 and S5 can gather only 2 votes (their own two) but need 3, so they cannot elect a leader or commit anything. S4 may bump its term to 3, but it can never win with it. Real systems add a pre-vote check so an isolated server does not inflate its term and disturb the leader when the network heals. The minority refuses to answer rather than risk two conflicting histories. That is the consistency choice from the CAP lesson.
steps.idea: Only the side with a majority can make progress, so a partition can never produce two committed histories.
steps.caption: S4 and S5 are isolated and cannot commit.

steps.title: What etcd and ZooKeeper do
steps.body: You rarely write Raft yourself. etcd (which uses Raft) and ZooKeeper (which uses a similar protocol called Zab) run a small cluster of 3 or 5 servers holding a small amount of critical data: configuration, who is the leader of a service, cluster membership, locks. Kubernetes keeps all of its state in etcd. These stores are slow for bulk data, because every write pays a round trip to a majority. Use them for coordination, not for your application's rows.
steps.idea: Use consensus stores for small, high-value coordination data, never as your main database.
steps.caption: A client reads and writes small coordination data.

steps.title: Agreement by majority
steps.body: Raft elects one leader per numbered term. The leader copies each log entry to followers and commits it once a majority has stored it. A new leader needs a majority of votes, and those voters must hold every committed entry, so committed data survives leader crashes. A minority side stalls instead of diverging. The price is a majority round trip on every write, so use it for small coordination data.
steps.idea: Majority plus terms gives one history. The costs are a round trip per write and no progress without a majority.
steps.caption: Leader, terms, majority commit, safe failover.

quiz.q: A Raft cluster has 5 servers. The leader has stored an entry itself, and one follower has also stored it. Can the leader tell the client the write is committed?
options: Yes, two copies is enough to survive one crash
No, it needs at least 3 of 5 servers to hold the entry
Yes, because the leader's own copy is authoritative
No, it needs all 5 servers to hold the entry
quiz.why: Commit requires a majority, 3 of 5. With only 2 copies, the other three servers could form a majority, elect a leader without the entry, and the write would be lost.

quiz.q: Why must a server refuse to vote for a candidate whose log is behind its own?
options: To keep elections short
To stop the old leader from restarting
To prevent followers from voting twice in a term
To make sure the winner already holds every committed entry
quiz.why: Any committed entry sits on a majority, and any winning candidate also needs a majority of votes. The overlapping server blocks candidates that lack the entry.

quiz.q: A 6-server cluster is split into groups of 3 and 3 by a network failure. What happens?
options: Both groups elect leaders and keep accepting writes
The group containing the old leader keeps working
Neither group can reach a majority of 4, so neither can commit
The group with the lowest server IDs wins automatically
quiz.why: A majority of 6 is 4. With 3 and 3, neither side has it, so writes stall. This is also why odd cluster sizes are preferred.

quiz.q: The leader of term 1 was frozen by a long pause. Meanwhile S3 won term 2. When the old leader resumes, it still thinks it leads and tries to send an entry. What happens?
options: Followers reject it because its term is lower, and it steps down
Followers accept it if it has more entries than S3
Followers accept it because it arrived last
Followers start a new election in term 1
quiz.why: A paused or partitioned leader can still believe it leads. Servers reject messages from a lower term, and a leader that sees a higher term immediately becomes a follower. Terms keep stale leaders harmless.

quiz.q: Which workload is a poor fit for storing directly in etcd or ZooKeeper?
options: Service leader and membership info
A cluster's feature-flag configuration
Millions of per-user order rows with heavy write traffic
A distributed lock's ownership record
quiz.why: Every write goes through a single leader and waits for a quorum, and the whole dataset is replicated to each server. Coordination state is small, but bulk application data should live in a scalable database.

cheatsheet.def: Getting a group of machines to agree on one value or one ordered history even when some crash or messages are lost.
Numbered election period in Raft. At most one leader per term; a higher term always overrides a lower one.
More than half the servers: floor(N/2)+1. A cluster of 2f+1 servers survives f failures.
A leader may report an entry committed once a majority has stored it durably. Never earlier.
How long a follower waits without a heartbeat before running for leader. Randomized per server to avoid ties; must exceed the heartbeat interval by a wide margin.
A server only votes for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, so the winner has every committed entry.
Small, strongly consistent stores built on Raft (etcd) or Zab (ZooKeeper). Used for config, leader election, membership and locks, not bulk data.
Use 3 or 5 servers. Even sizes add cost without adding failure tolerance, and more servers make every write slower.
